items.content: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

items.title:
There's panic right now that AI is eating indie software. I see it differently.
 
For 10+ years you could spin up a few
items.content:
There's panic right now that AI is eating indie software. I see it differently.
 
For 10+ years you could spin up a few hundred auto-generated pages, rank them, and let Google send you signups for free. 

Now the answer people used to click your site for sits right inside ChatGPT and Google's AI overviews. 

If your whole business ran on that one faucet, the water's turning off, and it feels like the end of the world.

And I've built a few of these projects, so I feel that darkness too.

But let's look at the data. Has it really gotten dark/worse for software founders and indie devs??

Let's look a Stripe Data...

New companies on Stripe Atlas are up 130% year over year. Companies are hitting $10M ARR within three months of launch at double last year's rate. One in five charges its first customer inside the first month, up from 8% in 2020. Fastest business formation anyone's ever recorded!!

And the solopreneurs, the exact people saying they're getting crushed, are winning the most. 

63% of new companies on Atlas are solo founded, and AI native solo startups pull 2.3x the revenue by month 24. This category was basically non existent at the scale we're seeing rn like 5 years ago.

TLDR;

So my thinking it's a channel shift wearing a collapse costume. The people hurting share one setup: they sell inexpensive tools to other indie hackers, and/or their traffic comes from SEO. 

That's the most exposed spot in the whole market, because your customers can rebuild your $20 SaaS in a weekend, and your traffic source is the exact thing the models replaced. Kinda feels like 2 cannons pointed at one little boat.

Call me an optimist, but here's my take....

Building software is a bigger game than it's ever been. 

More companies, forming faster, making money sooner, run by fewer people, than any point in history.

items.content:
People are wasting their AI subscriptions.

They don’t realize how powerful AI can be in achieving their own goals. 

They’re asking AI to reply to emails with zero goals in mind and nothing laddering up to “the big picture”. 

I was that kid where if my parents asked me to clean my room, I wouldn’t do it. 

They could tell me royalty was coming over, and I still wouldn’t do it. 

But if they said, “Bet you can’t clean your room in the next 5 minutes!”, that place would be spotless. 

When things are gamified and it becomes a personal challenge against myself, I am bought IN. 

I use that trick with AI today. 

Anything that feels tedious but really gets me closer to achieving my goals, I just make Claude build me a gaming interface to get it done. 

Oh you have to provide feedback on roundtable interview questions? Great. The interface is gray with canons and arrows as decoration. A knight is in the background, riding toward a castle to save his horse’s best donkey friend. Every question you fix and/or approve, the knight gets closer to the donkey. If you finish in under 6 minutes, the donkey is saved. And if you complete it this week instead of next week, he can save 100 donkeys. 

Hack your brain with AI. 

Consider the actual way you’ve been motivated in the past (yes, even if it’s insane to admit) and ask Claude/Codex to reorient its own work toward that motivation style.

items.content:
Nice chart!
A few remarks:
1. MAE (like other auto-encoders) is based on pixel reconstruction. It's expensive, doesn't scale well, and the representation quality is disappointing. 
2. I-JEPA doesn't have much in common with MAE (aside from explicit masking). It's more similar to DINO (it uses EMA) but has a predictor, since the latent prediction task is non symmetric. 
3. SimCLR (like Siamese nets (1993), DrLim (2005/2006)) is sample-contrastive. The other methods are not. The issue is that it requires very large batches and hard negative mining, and doesn't scale well with the dimension of the representation. Some methods, like Swav, Deep cluster, DINOs, are also contrastive but between learned clusters.

LOOP ENGINEERING IS THE SHIFT FROM AGENTS WAITING FOR YOUR NEXT MESSAGE TO AGENTS RUNNING THEMSELVES.

Addy Osmani's framework breaks it into five technical structures.

Automation. Scheduled triggers, cron jobs checking for CI failures or triaging issues, no human starting the process.

Git worktrees. Agents working on separate branches in parallel without stepping on each other's changes.

Skills. Job-specific know-how stored as markdown files, so an agent understands the nuances of a specific task without you re-explaining it every time.

Plugins and connectors. Integration with Notion, Stripe, MCP, extending an agent past its own local environment.

Sub-agents. A main agent breaking work into pieces and deploying sub-agents to execute them, with the added benefit of one agent verifying another's work.

The real shift is human-led to agent-led. The real risk is compounding errors as autonomy grows. Checks and balances are not optional, they're what keeps this a net positive instead of a liability.

Anything below the bar spins up a child session that fixes it and opens a PR.

The part nobody tells you: the setup isn't technical. 

You just talk to your agent.

- Pick the most important surface in your app. 
- Tell it how to judge good vs. bad. 
- Tell it to run daily. 
- Tell it to fix what fails.

That's it. That's the self-improvement loop.

And what it catches is the stuff I'd never fix myself, the tiny UX paper cuts where I'd look at the ticket and go, meh, are we really shipping a fix for that?

Turns out the answer is yes.

Because the work is already done.

You do this by understanding the current state, the reasoning, the implementation, taking the next step, learning its limitations, and improving over time.

/loop is the most useful Claude Code command.

If you're still confused about how to run your first loop, read this.

You have two options for running effective loops:

Option 1. Standard Prompting (the easiest way to start)

Open Claude Code (or desktop) and type /loop

On desktop, you'll see a caption field pop up (optional). From there, just type your goal.

Example:

/loop do some research on the robotics sector - I'm looking for some potential investment opportunities and basic exposure.

This runs until the goal is met, then stops on its own.

Option 2. Scheduled Loops

Standard prompting stops once the goal is met - but sometimes you want a loop that keeps checking in on a repeating basis instead of running just once.

Add a time interval to your /loop command, and it keeps repeating on that schedule until you tell it to stop.

This is how you set up real recurring workflows.

/loop [time interval], [your goal]

Example:

/loop everyday at 9am do [x]

Save this so you can actually deploy effective loops.

items.content:
If you already knew all 26 hacks, unfollow me.

Almost nobody makes it past Claude hack 8:

(#3 is me deleting my own past advice):

1. Use the Claude Desktop app. The browser is the demo. The app is where Cowork lives.

2. Use Cowork, not the chatbot. If you're typing into a chat box, you're using it like it's 2025.

3. Forget .md files & folders. Folders leak old outputs into your context, and nobody on Earth maintains those files weekly.

4. Skills and Projects. That's the entire system now. A skill is a capability you teach once. A project is a place you go back to.

5. Delete your about-me file. Rebuild it as a skill so it follows you into every single chat.
✦ Don't know how to build one? Take mine:
✦ Go to https://t.co/psB7XxAv8w. Subscribe for free.
✦ Don't pay anything. Open my welcome email.
✦ Hit the automatic reply button inside.
✦ Open the Notion link. Go to "Claude skills".
✦ Download the library. Upload it in Customize.

6. Turn every setting off. Empty your global instructions. Leave Connectors on. That's it.

7. Projects remember between chats. And you can share one with your entire team in two clicks.

8. Here's where most people quit reading. The longer your chat, the dumber it gets. Anthropic's own engineers said it out loud.

9. So stop typing "no, I meant…". Click "Restart the conversation from here" on an earlier message. 

10. A token is roughly one word. Every word you send & receive is money. Message 30 costs you 31 times message 1.

11. Point Fable 5 at your single hardest problem. Two turns. Then switch models. Turns are the most expensive habit you have.

12. Opus 5 High for everything else. High, not Max.

13. Don't give Claude steps. Give it the goal & get out of the way. Steps drag it down to old Claude.

14. Don't paste logins, passwords, or keys. Ever.

15. Skills fire themselves. You don't prompt them. You type /command.

16. It will sound 100% sure when it's dead wrong.

17. Don't trust agreement either. Claude is a sycophant. Pleasing you and being right are two different jobs.

18. Use Research mode (the "+" in the chat box). Almost nobody knows it's in there. Give it something genuinely hard.

19. Add "use AskUserQuestion" to your prompt. Claude interviews you before it answers. It prompts itself better than you ever will.

20. Talk, don't type. Cowork reads 100,000 words in 15 secs, then waits for you at 60 words per minute. You speak at 150.

21. Ask for five very different versions. Then pick one. That part is taste, and taste is the part it can't do for you.

22. Make it audit its own answer before you trust a single line.

23. Feed it too much context and it goes in circles. Same answers every time, zero creativity. Keep the context in the project and the chat clean.

24. The first draft is yours to fix, not to ship. Always.

25. The only rule that matters: outsource the thinking, never the understanding.

Building an AI trading bot has literally never been easier.

Anyone with a laptop + WiFi and 10 minutes of free time can completely automate their trading with AI.

The full process (you'll want to save this):

Step 1. Understand the architecture

Whether you're trading stocks or crypto, every trading bot is built from the same two parts:
→ The brain: strategizes your trading. An LLM like Claude or Codex is best for this.
→ The hands: execute your trades. This happens through an MCP connection.

Step 2. Pick your MCP (stocks)

For stocks, one of my favorite MCPs is the Alpaca connector.

It's completely free and has paper trading built in, so you can test everything with fake money before risking real capital.

Step 3. Connect Alpaca (3 sub-steps)

→ Sign up for an Alpaca account
→ Grab your API key
→ Plug the API key into Claude

That's it. Your brain and your hands are now connected.

Step 4. Pick your MCP (crypto)

Same exact process, different exchange.

Go to your exchange (Blofin, Binance, Bybit, etc), grab your API key from your account settings.

Step 5. Connect your exchange

Plug the API key into Claude with a prompt like:

"I want to automate my trading with the Blofin MCP, connect my API key [insert key], and build a dashboard to manage my trading."

Once connected, your AI can read your positions, place trades, and manage everything from one interface.

Step 6. Dashboard build

From here, you can build a fully customizable dashboard trading terminal to manage your trading.

Pro tip: connect other MCPs to get live price data.

Such a simple setup and easy way to start automating your trading.

You're using Claude the wrong way for 80% of your SEO tasks. 

Here's exactly how to fix it:

1: You give Claude vague prompts.

Fix: "Analyze my site, find gaps vs competitors, and give me a plan to get more leads."

2: You don't load your full business context first.

Fix: Paste your services, locations, keywords, competitors, and ideal customers before anything else.

3: You treat Claude like a chatbot not a strategist.

Fix: Ask "What's blocking our organic growth right now?" not "Improve my SEO."

4: You skip competitor gap analysis.

Fix: "Compare my website with my top 3 competitors. Show me what they rank for that I don't."

5: You cluster keywords by volume not intent.

Fix: Group by informational, commercial, and transactional. Intent drives conversions.

6: You ignore AI search optimization.

Fix: "Why would AI recommend this business over competitors? What should I clarify or add?"  7: You never tell Claude your city or service area. 
Fix: Always include "[Service] in [City]" in every prompt. Claude doesn't know where you operate unless you tell it every single time.

8: You ask Claude to write content before doing keyword research. 
Fix: "Find me 10 high intent local keywords for [service] in [city] first. Then write content around the top 3."

9: You use Claude in Chat instead of Cowork.

Fix: Open Cowork. Select Opus 4.7. Turn on Extended Thinking. Wrong tab = surface level output every time.

10: You never check what your competitors are ranking for.

Fix: "Open Google and find the top 3 businesses ranking for [keyword] in [city]. Tell me every keyword gap between them and my site."

items.content:
your AI agent can watch any video now - paste a URL and it sees every frame, hears every word, all for free 🤯

bradautomates/claude-video gives Claude the ability to watch YouTube, Loom, TikTok, local files - anything yt-dlp supports

what people actually use it for:

→ analyze a competitor launch - what hook, what visuals, what structure
→ debug from a screen recording - Claude reads the exact frame where it breaks
→ summarize a 49-min talk in 30 seconds with frame-accurate timestamps
→ strip the hype from product videos - "what's actually new, skip the pitch"

the mechanism: yt-dlp pulls free captions first (zero cost). ffmpeg extracts frames at scene-aware intervals - not uniform sampling, so you don't waste tokens on 12 identical frames of the same slide. Claude reads every frame as an image with timestamp markers. Groq Whisper only kicks in when a video has no caption track

how to set up (3 min):

> claude code: /plugin marketplace add bradautomates/claude-video then /plugin install watch@claude-video
> or npx skills add bradautomates/claude-video -g for codex, cursor, gemini cli
> dependencies auto-install on macOS via brew

two caveats: free captions cover most but not all videos. past 10 min use --start/--end for focused sections or the token-burner mode for full coverage

Postiz is still growing by ~$1k/MRR per day ($165k MRR).
You can see proof here: 
https://t.co/AOCjAX5Bg4

I have seen so many B2B SaaS companies losing revenue, and a few that managed to grow past it.

Here is my conclusion, and I might be wrong.
In 2021, when COVID hit, SaaS was booming; tons of indie hackers had high MRR back then that was continuing to grow until 2024.

With AI just available to the public, people made the most generic AI SaaS (mass market). For example, image generators, Video Generators, etc.

But then, there were literally too many people who were doing it, even huge companies like Jasper that raised $100m+

Most of those indies stopped innovating since then.
Usually innovation is not making new features, but actually changing your product or at least your product marketing message.

For example: Postiz changed from a social media scheduling tool to an agent running your social media.
In the main marketing message - not as a feature.

Also, distribution became much harder - hence why people are leaning towards VC money.

Take Higgsfield for example - they are just a Seedance wrapped with an application layer, but their marketing is super aggressive, possible only by funded companies.

So what happened since 2021:
1. "Building in public" was a super interesting thing; everybody wanted to learn about it. Now, it's less effective. You might get tons of views but not many subscriptions.

2. SEO for mass-market products became really hard, as there are tons of those, and it would be really hard to get into the first places on the SERP.

3. Same for ads: more people are bidding, and CAC goes up.

What I think people need to do:
1. Be innovative. One obvious reason is to build for agents because it's easy. If you can implement deep tech, it's also good.

2. Sell the outcome - usually the more niche you get, the easier it is to focus on your use case, so instead of selling "Social media for agents", sell "How to make money by automating your TikTok". Because then people don't buy you because of the software; they buy you because they want to go viral, and that changes the whole mechanism of - everybody can vibe code this.

3. Find other channels to sell it - if you already see that you are failing again and again on X and SEO, you can definitely look for other solutions. Organic content became easier than it was before. Many platforms moved from follower-based to interest-based. You can go viral on TikTok without having a lot of followers. You will have to investigate.

4. Understand the new distribution world - LLMs are now the 1st search engine. How can you rank in AEO? You have to figure it out. And no, it's not just by doing SEO - actually, it can be much, much easier. The most cited websites are Reddit / LinkedIn, and YouTube. Literally, by commenting to people there, LLMs can find you.

5. List yourself in places for distribution - did you know that you can list yourself in the ChatGPT marketplace, Claude marketplace, etc. for both skills and connectors? Postiz already got 2m downloads there.

Final thoughts:
Is it harder? yes.
Is it possible? yes.

If I did it, everybody can do it.

items.title:
Your Ceiling Is Delegation

@jess__yan , product lead for Claude Managed Agents, Anthropic, interviewed by @petergyang
items.content:
Your Ceiling Is Delegation

@jess__yan , product lead for Claude Managed Agents, Anthropic, interviewed by @petergyang  (Behind the Craft)

Summary: Jess Yan leads Claude Managed Agents at Anthropic, and her core claim is that agents have crossed from prompting loops into autonomous, long-running coworkers you can load with work overnight. How much you can delegate at once now caps your output more than your personal capacity does. The fastest path to value is making one person exponentially more powerful, then scaling from there.

1. From Loops To Coworkers. Agents stopped being prompting loops and became autonomous, self-recovering, long-running actors. Once they were just question-and-answer loops; now they hold permissions, access to internal tooling and sensitive data, memory, and the judgment to know when to keep going versus ask a human. The harness, meaning the scaffolding around the model that runs tools, calls memory, and decides when to pull a human in, is what turns raw token-sampling into a product. As the tasks get more ambitious, the harness gets thicker while the prompt stays simple.

2. The Ceiling Is Delegation. The new limit on what you get done is how much you can delegate at once. Yan puts it directly: the limits of what we can achieve will be based on how much we can delegate, more than on our personal capacities. The working model is to set tasks overnight and wake up to a resolved backlog and squashed bugs. Load agents up with work the way you would brief a partner.

3. Outcome Is The New Output. Structured outputs used to mean forcing rigid JSON and gluing it together by hand. Now the outcome itself is the spec: describe the rich, interactive thing you want and let the agent self-correct its way there. Yan calls this a tastemaker's assessment of what good looks like. You set the standard, the agent iterates to hit it, grinding a predictive model until it clears 90% accuracy. The skill shifts from writing formatting instructions to defining the standard.

4. Empower The Individual First. The mistake enterprises make is jumping straight to automating a 20-team, multi-month workflow. Yan's counter is to make one person exponentially more powerful first, giving them agents that do the design work or handle the dependency request they would have waited on a human for. You end up with a bunch of one-person startups inside a large company. Raise the ceiling on what individuals can ship alone, then go after the mega-processes.

5. Spin Up, Throw Away. Treat agents as disposable. Yan keeps a different agent running every couple of weeks, each suited to the task of the moment, and discards it when the need passes. One example: a 4,000-org waitlist full of duplicates and junk, where she built an agent with access to internal systems to parse it, score who was likely to convert, and pull people in daily, knowing the whole thing would be obsolete in a few weeks. It does not have to be productized. It has to work now.

6. Vibe Test Before You Eval. Get the agent into real users' hands before building formal evals. Yan says vibe testing is the most important first step. You outgrow it once you cannot aggregate vibe signals at scale, and that is when evals come in: binary pass/fail, LLM-as-judge scoring, and triggering evals that check a specific action actually fired. Do not burn weeks on eval scaffolding before anyone has touched the thing.

7. Agents Grading Agents. Let agents evaluate their own work, ideally in a separate context window to avoid bias. Claude Managed Agents can pull the eval loop directly into the session, so the agent grades its outputs and revises before a human ever looks. Yan's own loop mirrors what builders do in Claude Code: generate, have another agent judge, regenerate if the grade is bad. Self-correction inside the loop beats stringing together human checkpoints.

8. Always-On Agents. A real coworker does not wait to be asked. Yan runs agents that monitor Slack channels, summarize customer activity, and surface things on their own through triggered events and cron jobs, constantly refreshing context so they stay as current as she is. The two sources of power are the level of data access you grant and an interaction style she describes as humanlike and proactive. An always-on agent has to pop up at the right time, in the place the work already lives.

9. I Talk To Claude More Than Coworkers. Yan admits she talks to Claude more than her teammates, spending therapy time wrapping her head around thorny concepts before a meeting. The effect is that she arrives with a real opinion and baseline research already done, so conversations with colleagues start at a deeper level. Anthropic even tags Claude into API design reviews as a neutral judge when the team hits an impasse. The agent uplevels human conversations rather than replacing them.

10. SaaS Goes Hyper-Vertical. As models absorb broad domain expertise, the value moves to incredibly specific, niche use cases. Picture an accounting agent built just for solopreneurs. The durable shared asset becomes context patterns and task-orchestration patterns that travel across these narrow agents. The products that survive are the ones that meet users exactly where their workflow already lives.

11. Software Lives In Chat And Code. The interface is collapsing into chat and the coding environment. Yan's point: you bring your personal agent, loaded with your contacts and context, and let it go deal with someone else's agent, instead of filling out forms on a website. Everyone is becoming an engineering team, so work increasingly lives in Claude Code and in chat. Build where the agents already are.

items.content:
Just watched @asmartbear teardown @dmytrokrasun's $32k/mo screenshot API (9% churn)

Jason laid out Options A-D:
- Option A: Optimize baseline
- Option B: Build a marketing tool
- Option C: Sell the business
- Option D: Go all-in on MCP / AI

I think Jason missed the best strategy

There’s an "Option E" that is even better 👇

Why not Option D (MCP / AI):

Dmytro noted at 1h:31m that desktop agents already have browser access. Jason brushed it off as a sales objection, but Dmytro is right:

1. Local browsers are free & instant
Cursor, Claude Code, and Windsurf spin up isolated Playwright instances (0ms latency, $0 cost). No 3rd-party API needed for prompts.

2. Static PNGs vs. interactive DOM
Agents don't just need a picture, they click buttons, fill forms, and wait for DOM states. If you need cloud execution, you buy browser infra (@browser_use), not a screenshot API.

3. The "security" argument is backwards
Jason argued local agents get access to "your email and bank". But Playwright launches fresh ephemeral profiles with zero cookies or saved sessions.

Plus, 3rd-party APIs can't reach internal or staging URLs behind a corporate VPN anyway. Local IS the enterprise-safe option.

4. ScreenshotOne’s real moat
It’s not LLM chat prompts, it’s background execution and automation at scale (anti-bot bypass, Cloudflare evasion, 500 parallel renders). That’s how I use it at https://t.co/fiqqEJPjZ6 for web scraping and https://t.co/X5gQf8nHsk for brand identity.

Why Option B (Jason’s version) falls short:

Jason suggested reusing screenshot code for a marketing regression tool, but Dmytro is burned out on screenshots.

The real asset isn't screenshot code. It's DISTRIBUTION.

Dmytro has:
- 1,000 paying B2B customers
- Domain Rating of 62 (DR 62)
- #1 ranking high-intent search traffic

🏆 Option E: Launch SaaS #2 to the same audience

1. Analyze the full workflow
What do users do right before or after screenshots?
- Cold email teams need contact email enrichment
- AI devs need HTML → Clean Markdown for LLMs
- QA teams need visual regression diffs

2. Sell a 2nd full-priced subscription
Don't add cheap $5 add-ons. Launch a 2nd standalone API at a full $30–$50/mo.

3. $0 CAC expansion MRR
Starting from zero means 12 months grinding backlinks. SaaS #2 gets instant cross-sells from 1k paid users + DR 62 search leads on Day 1.

Write listicles & "how-to" guides on ScreenshotOne that rank immediately for adjacent API keywords.

4. Cures founder burnout safely
Fresh product momentum backed by a $30k/mo cash-flow safety net.

Option E is the ONLY play that fits Dmytro’s psychological state on the call:

- Option A makes him feel "tired" & "not super excited"
- 5 more years of it feels like "there's so much more to do"
- Option C (selling) would be a "painful experience... from zero"

SaaS #2 gives him new-build energy without from-zero pain: new problem, new market, new landing page, backed by 1,000 customers and a ranked domain.

TL;DR: Keep App #1 on maintenance ➔ Analyze workflows ➔ Launch SaaS #2 to your current audience.

THIS SOLO FOUNDER IS SHIPPING 22-25 PRs A DAY BY MANAGING AI AGENTS LIKE EMPLOYEES

Ryan Carson built Treehouse, taught 1M people to code, sold the company, and now runs Untangle as basically a one-person AI startup.

his new skill is not prompting.

it's managing a software factory.

the setup:

> Devon cloud agents instead of local worktrees - 5 to 10 isolated coding environments running at once
> 52-inch monitor with 8 screens open - every agent thread visible like a mini engineering team
> Slack only for agent notifications - the founder becomes the unblocker, not the typist
> 1Password for prod keys - agents never get production write access unless he manually approves it
> phone-first workflow - more than 50% of the company gets managed from mobile
> pinned high-stakes threads - checked every ~25 minutes so the important agents don't drift

the crazy part is the automation layer.

every morning at 9am, a production watchdog scans paid customer activity, summarizes what happened in JSON, and links directly into the admin UI.

then another agent reviews conversations between their AI paralegal “Grace” and real law firm users.

if the score drops below the rubric, it spins up a child coding session and fixes the product.

Ryan says they ship around 3 of these tiny UX fixes per day automatically.

this is the real 2026 skill gap:

most people are still learning how to write better prompts.

the top 1% are learning how to run 10 agents, route tasks between models, protect production, review PRs, and make 20 high-stakes decisions before lunch.

prompt engineering was the tutorial level.

agent management is the job.

bookmark this before your “AI workflow” turns into an actual engineering org
